Netanyahu orders preparation of possible legal case against Erdogan, report says
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has ordered an interministerial team and a senior Justice Ministry official to prepare a legal case against Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, i24NEWS reported on Sunday.
The order followed Erdogan’s announcement that Turkey had asked Interpol to issue a red notice for Netanyahu, the report said.
Israel could itself seek to bring the case before the International Criminal Court in The Hague, which issued an arrest warrant for Netanyahu in 2024 on charges of war crimes and crimes against humanity allegedly committed in Gaza since October 2023.
Israel is, however, more likely to pursue the case through a third party, if it filed one at all, the report said, adding that it could instead use the proposed case to pressure Erdogan.
The case would focus on Israel’s allegations concerning Erdogan’s government’s relationship with Hamas and the Kurdish groups, amid a renewed peace process between Turkish government and the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK).
The report follows Netanyahu’s speech to the UN General Assembly on Friday, in which he called Erdogan a “tyrant”.
In response, a Turkish official called Netanyahu’s remarks “desperate and empty attempts” to cover up "Israel’s genocide" in Gaza and its ongoing attacks on the occupied West Bank, Lebanon, Syria and elsewhere.

After being unlawfully detained in October 2013 for being close to a protest, and categorised as an alleged Muslim Brotherhood "terrorist" (read: protester), he found himself interned in Egypt's spiralling archipelago of political prisons, along with his father.

Contrary to popular understanding, an assault in law is not an act of violence itself, but the apprehension that unlawful violence might take place - and nothing better describes life in Egypt's prisons than a constant assault.

Iraq seeks US exemption from sanctions on Iranian airlines
The Iraqi government has said it is in talks with the United States to seek an exemption from sanctions on Iranian airlines, which have disrupted travel for patients, students and pilgrims.
All Iraqi airports enforced the US ban this week, resulting in major disruption at the airport serving the holy city of Najaf, the main destination in Iraq for Iranian flights.
"The Iraqi government is holding direct talks with the American side to exempt certain Iraqi airports from these measures," the prime minister's media office said.
An exemption, it added, would allow flights to resume "for humanitarian reasons, including medical treatment, education, religious visits, and for the interest of civilians".
Iranian airlines mainly carry Iraqi Shia pilgrims to Iran's holy cities or Iranians visiting sacred sites in Iraq. The flights also serve Iraqi students studying in Iran and patients seeking medical treatment there.
In an interview with Iranian news agency ISNA, Iran's ambassador to Iraq Mohammad Kazem Al-Sadegh said his country was also in contact with the Baghdad authorities to find a way to restore the flights.
"There are roughly 25 daily flights from Iran to Najaf and about 15 flights to Baghdad, and... around 12,000 to 13,000 people travel between Iran and Iraq and vice versa on Iranian airlines, which is not a small number," he said.

Riyadh schools to operate remotely for week, AFP reports
Parents across Riyadh received emails from schools on Sunday announcing a last-minute plan to shift to remote learning for a week, according to messages seen by AFP.
"We have just been informed by Saudi authorities that schools must remain closed all week," read two separate messages seen by AFP.
There was no official reason given but the move comes amid heightened tensions in the Gulf and near-daily attacks aimed at Saudi Arabia by Iran-backed Houthi fighters in Yemen.
"When a decision affects an entire school community for a full week, families deserve clear communication and transparency about the reasons behind it," one parent living in Riyadh who spoke on condition of anonymity told AFP.
"It's a last-minute decision. We have no clue what's happening," a Lebanese expatriate living in Riyadh added.
The announcement comes a day after the Saudi-led coalition battling Yemen's Houthis said it had intercepted drones and ballistic missiles targeting the kingdom.
The strikes were the latest in a series of escalating Houthi attacks since July, when renewed hostilities shattered a years-long truce and embroiled Yemen in the wider Middle East war.
The United Nations Security Council earlier condemned escalating attacks on Saudi Arabia by Houthi fighters, noting that the strikes have wounded "civilians, including women and children".
Report by AFP

Israeli police 'reopen' probe into pepper-spray attack on Armenian boy
Israeli police have reopened investigation into the pepper-spraying of a nine-year-old Armenian Christian boy in Jerusalem, after closing it despite the assault being capture on security cameras, according to Israeli journalist Yossi Eli.
"Following my exposé and the shock from what happened to William, the police have reopened the case and will collect the cameras. If this weren't so sad, it would be gratifying that the police only work like this," Eli wrote on X.
The boy, identified only as William, was riding his bicycle near the Mamilla neighbourhood on Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar, while listening to music through headphones.

A video shared by Eli shows William seen crying inside an ambulance as his mother reassures him that his younger sister, Arev, is safe.
Eli reported that this was the second attack on William. In the first, he was accompanied by his father, who intervened to protect him; this time, he was alone.

At least 30 men have been executed in eastern Libya since late August after being sentenced to death in secretive military trials and at least 50 others remain at imminent risk of execution, local media and rights groups have reported over the last week.
Amnesty International said the Libyan Arab Armed Forces (LAAF), led by eastern commander Khalifa Haftar and the de facto authorities in the region, resumed executions on 23 August in Libya for the first time since 2010.
Those executed had been convicted following “grossly unfair and secretive trials” marred by torture, the rights group said.
Some of those executed or still awaiting death sentences were convicted of murder and terrorism-related offences linked to fighting between the LAAF and opposing armed groups between 2014 and 2018, Amnesty said.
Several detainees claimed to have been tortured by armed groups affiliated with the LAAF following their arrests, including to obtain “confessions” that were later used as evidence against them, the rights group said.
“The LAAF authorities must immediately halt all executions,” the organisation said, calling for a moratorium and the overturning of convictions and death sentences handed down following unfair trials.
Amnesty also called on authorities to retry civilians accused of internationally recognised criminal offences in accordance with international standards of fairness in civilian courts that do not use evidence obtained through torture.
It called on authorities to grant international monitors access to Gernada and other detention sites in eastern Libya.

Burnham's arrival as the premier has injected new energy and hope into the Labour membership, as well as the parliamentary party itself.
Polling shows that Labour is starting to regain some of the voters who had abandoned it in droves under Starmer for Reform UK on the right and the Green Party on the left.

All eyes are on Burnham to use the conference to unveil a bold and comprehensive new vision for the government.

UN expands list of companies operating in West Bank settlements
The United Nations human rights office issued a list on Friday adding 61 more companies operating in Israeli West Bank settlements, which are illegal under international law.
The database is highly sensitive as firms could be targeted for boycotts or divestment to pressure Israel over settler expansion in the territory that is home to over three million Palestinians.
The database, first released in 2020, now includes 214 firms, mostly from Israel, but also from 10 other countries including France, Germany, China and the US.
Newly added firms included Israeli pesticides maker ADAMA, part of Chinese-owned Syngenta Group, Israel-based real estate investment holding company Alony Hetz and Spain's Salvat Logistica.
They did not immediately respond to a request for comment on their inclusion in the UN database.
They joined companies such as travel agency Expedia and home-rental company Airbnb already on the list.
